newsitem.title: FRANCE: 34 hurt in blaze in Channel Tunnel freight train.
newsitem.headline: 34 hurt in blaze in Channel Tunnel freight train.

text.p: Thirty-four people were injured, two seriously, in a fire and choking toxic fumes aboard a train carrying trucks through the Channel Tunnel between Britain and France, officials said on Tuesday.
The accident, which forced the closure of the tunnel, was the worst since the 51-km (32-mile) undersea rail link opened two years ago.
A total of eight people were taken to hospital. The rest were given treatment for varying degrees of smoke inhalation.

Fire-fighters from France and Britain in special breathing gear brought the fire under control 17 kms (10 miles) from the French mouth of the tunnel early on Tuesday, after eight hours. The blaze was reported to have started in a truck carrying a load of inflamable polystyrene.

French state-owned railway SNCF said Eurostar passenger express services between Paris and London were suspended as was the Le Shuttle service for trucks and cars between Calais in France and Folkstone on the British side.

SNCF and Franco-British operator Eurotunnel SA Plc hoped to reopen the tunnel during the day after removal of the damaged train. Passengers booked on cancelled services were offered seats on planes or ferries.

"Thirty-four people were affected, both passengers and train staff. The two most seriously injured were taken by helicopter to Lille hospital (near Calais) but their lives are not in danger," said Jean-Pascal Cogez, deputy prefect in Calais.
"Six passengers were hospitalised in Calais and 26 others were placed under medical surveillance after inhaling smoke," he told Reuters.
All the truck drivers, who were riding in a lounge car in the shuttle, were evacuated initially through a service tunnel. The first fire-fighters arrived within about 10 minutes.

The cause of the fire, which spread to three other trucks in the train, was unknown. A legal probe would be opened in France into the blaze, the latest in a series of woes for the tunnel, dogged by cost over-runs and fierce competition from ferries.
The freight shuttle train was halted and evacuated between 9 and 10 p.m. (same GMT).

Mady Chabrier, a spokeswoman for Eurotunnel, said: "The fire is under control but the train is still too hot. We hope to pull it out later today. We could use a parallel tunnel but for the moment it is being used by firemen."
She could not confirm media reports that the fire started in a lorry carrying polysterene, an inflammable material.
When reopened, the tunnel would be reduced for a while to a single track from its normal twin north-south tracks.
The fire started at the back of the 730 metre (yard) long train, which has locomotives at front and back and can carry up to 28 large trucks, a Eurotunnel spokeswoman said in London.
"It is the first time the tunnel has been closed for an emergency. We have had safety drills in the past but this is the first real event," she said.
The passengers and crew were evacuated from the northbound tunnel to a central service shaft and then transported via another shuttle train back to France via the southbound tunnel.

Crews in breathing gear rotated in shifts to tackle the dense smoke and searing heat generated by the fire in the narrow confines of the tunnel. Firefighters used a freshwater main running the length of the tunnel to douse the flames.

"Firefighters are basically having to feel their way along the tunnel and they can only stay down there for a maximum of 10 minutes before we have to bring them back because of the heat," said commander Bill Welsh of the Kent County fire brigade.
"The heat is so intense and all the lights have gone out and there is falling debris everywhere but crews on both sides are working very well together," he said.
